findings.reason: Confirmed (high). The published article (p. 8, between Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2) says 'Let y = Spec κ be a geometric point of X//G. We may identify the fibre X_y with a closed G-invariant subscheme of X.' Item /001 copies it. The counterexample is right. With G_m acting trivially on X = A¹_k, X//G = X; at the geometric generic point, X_y = Spec of an algebraic closure of k(t), whose image in X is the non-closed generic point. More generally X_y is a κ-scheme, so it is a subscheme of X only when κ = κ(y). What holds is a closed G_κ-invariant immersion X_y → X ×_S Spec κ: the κ-point of (X//G)_κ is a closed immersion, since (X//G)_κ is separated over κ. Lemma 2.2's proof works on X_y as a κ-scheme and is unaffected. The fix is right.

Confirmed (high). Lemma 3.35 (p. 24) assumes only that the image of 𝔭 lies in P₁R, and its proof says 'Since A is finitely generated over R, κ(𝔭) is a finite extension of κ(𝔭′)'. That is false. Take R = k[[t]], A = R[x] and 𝔭 = (0): the contraction (0) lies in P₁R, but κ(𝔭) = k((t))(x) is transcendental over k((t)). The cotangent argument is right. Over K = κ(𝔭), the k-derivations ∂_t (continuous on k[[t]]) and ∂_x of A into K extend K-linearly to two independent derivations of B_𝔮 into K at the residue map. So 𝔮/𝔮² has dimension at least 2, and the completion cannot be Â_𝔭⟦T⟧ = K⟦T⟧. The applications (Corollary 3.38, Proposition 4.9) are at closed points, where κ(𝔭) is finite over κ(𝔭′). The fix, adding that hypothesis and recording a sourceIssue, is right.
